analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurers to cover all COVID-19 care with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced days after COVID-19 was declared a national emergency, was referred to three House committees and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every private health plan to pay the full cost of COVID-19 testing, treatment, hospital care, prescription drugs, and vaccines, with no cost-sharing for patients. It also would have opened a special enrollment window letting anyone diagnosed with COVID-19 sign up for coverage immediately, instead of waiting for the annual open-enrollment season. It was introduced on March 19, 2020, the same month COVID-19 shut down the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with private insurance who got COVID-19 would avoid deductibles and copays that often run into thousands of dollars for a hospital stay. Uninsured people diagnosed with COVID-19 could enroll in a plan on the spot, so their treatment would be covered going forward. Employers' plans and marketplaces would have to process these enrollments year-round.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and individual and group insurance to cover outpatient and inpatient services for diagnosing, treating, and preventing COVID-19 — including tests, supportive care, vaccines, prescription drugs, medical devices, and hospital care — with no cost sharing at all, retroactive to plan years starting January 1, 2020.

Creates a special enrollment period so a person (or an eligible family member) who is diagnosed with or has a presumptive positive COVID-19 test can enroll immediately in an employer plan, a marketplace plan, or an exchange plan, starting the day the diagnosis is reported — instead of waiting until the next open enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies would bear the cost of every COVID-19 claim with no patient cost-sharing, and would take on newly enrolled members mid-year. Employers funding group plans would absorb part of the added claims cost.

drawbacks.text: Insurers would pay the full cost of all COVID-19 care with no patient cost-sharing, which drives up premiums for everyone in the plan rather than concentrating the bill on those who use care.

A special enrollment window triggered by diagnosis could invite people to buy coverage only after they get sick, which weakens the insurance pool and can push premiums up for everyone else — a problem the bill addresses only by letting the Secretary write timing rules.
The mandate applies retroactively to plan years beginning January 1, 2020, forcing plans to reprocess months of claims mid-pandemic.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing a disease that could mean weeks in intensive care, the benefit of guaranteed zero-cost treatment is large and direct. The costs — somewhat higher premiums spread across all enrollees and new mid-year enrollment churn — are real but modest by comparison, and the bill left the details of enrollment timing to the Secretary. The main design weakness is that it does nothing for the uninsured beyond letting them enroll after a diagnosis, which comes with a premium bill many sick people could not pay.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced and none of them ever acted on it, so it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raul Ruiz introduced the bill on March 19, 2020, with Rep. Tom Malinowski as its cosponsor, ten days after COVID-19 was declared a national emergency.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees, on the day of introduction.

It was referred to the Health Subcommittee on March 19, 2020, and no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Congress ultimately did address COVID-19 insurance coverage through other legislation that session, including free testing requirements in the broader coronavirus relief packages.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers were spared a mandate to pick up the full tab for COVID-19 treatment, and millions of patients went on paying deductibles and copays for COVID-19 care during the worst waves of the pandemic.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to read; both supporters in the record were Democrats, and the committees that sat on the bill were chaired by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill forces them to pay every COVID-19 claim with no patient cost-sharing and to absorb mid-year enrollees, converting patient bills into insurer costs. Their interest in blocking it ran against patients facing hospital bills.

industries.industry: Employers that fund group health plans
industries.note: Their plans would have to cover COVID-19 care in full and process special enrollments, raising benefits costs — while their own sick employees would be covered and could enroll immediately.
With insurers required to pay in full, hospitals would collect from insurers instead of chasing patients for large unpaid bills during a pandemic.

industries.industry: Uninsured individuals newly enrolling through marketplaces and employer plans
industries.note: The special enrollment period routes newly diagnosed people into coverage, giving insurers new paying members even as it gives patients access to care.
